data.title: Gábrišová at Varín – a Púchov culture hillfort above the Železná studňa ironworks
data.excerpt: In 2020 the Regional Monuments Board and the Považie Museum in Žilina, together with our civic association Hradiská, carried out a metal-detector survey at Gábrišová, a small fortified site of the Púchov culture that had been unknown until shortly before. Two bronze amulets, a ploughshare unique in the Žilina Basin and an unmatched number of structural fittings suggest that the craftsmen who smelted haematite at the nearby Železná studňa lived here.
data.metaTitle: Gábrišová at Varín – a Púchov culture hillfort
data.metaDescription: Gábrišová near Nezbudská Lúčka and Varín, a hillfort of the Púchov culture found by metal-detector survey in 2020, with two unusual bronze amulets.

keyFacts.label: Area of the fortification
keyFacts.value: approximately 0.5 ha – a size typical of fortifications of the Púchov culture in the upper Váh region

keyFacts.label: Occupation
keyFacts.value: both the pottery and the metal finds unambiguously confirm occupation by the Púchov culture

keyFacts.label: Bronze basket-shaped pendant
keyFacts.value: a Hallstatt type of amulet with Late La Tène elaboration; analogies at Liptovská Mara I-Havránok and Liptovská Mara III

keyFacts.label: Bronze figurine of a ram
keyFacts.value: a zoomorphic amulet with a suspension loop; only about 20 similar figurines are documented in Slovakia

keyFacts.label: A unique iron ploughshare
keyFacts.value: the only find of a narrow single-socketed ploughshare of this type in the whole Žilina Basin

keyFacts.label: Structural fittings
keyFacts.value: Gábrišová has the highest attested number of structural fittings among all sites of the Púchov culture

keyFacts.label: Heaps of metallurgical waste at Železná studňa
keyFacts.value: oval heaps measuring c. 15 × 23 m and up to 1.5 m high

keyFacts.label: Source of the iron ore
keyFacts.value: haematite from the Rechtorská dolina valley (the site of Rudy)

timeline.description: At the site of Strečno-Hradný vrch the remains of features with pottery dated to the B1 phase were recorded – the only hamlet so far known in the wider surroundings of Železná studňa.

mediaTexts.alt: A rocky ridge in a coniferous forest in the spring sunshine

children.text: In 2020 the Regional Monuments Board and the Považie Museum in Žilina, in cooperation with our civic association Hradiská, carried out a metal-detector survey at the site of Gábrišová, until recently unknown and so far unpublished, which extends on the boundary between the cadastral areas of the villages of Nezbudská Lúčka and Varín.
The site was published in the 2021 rigorosum thesis of the archaeologist Zuzana Staneková (1). The text below is for the most part taken over from that thesis.

The site of Nezbudská Lúčka/Varín-Gábrišová is a hilltop site extending above another known site – Železná studňa. A pronounced rocky ridge runs in a north–south direction. On the eastern side the slope of the ridge is steep and wind-exposed. On the opposite side, by contrast, the slope is sheltered from the wind, and the terracing of the slope indicates that in the past it was used for occupation. In terms of area the site belongs among the small defensive hillforts reaching about 0.5 ha, which is fairly typical of fortifications of the period of the Púchov culture in the upper Váh region. Its gentler slopes below the summit were modified into terraces. The archaeological finds are concentrated on two or three terraces of the western slope of Gábrišová. In the past the slope evidently suffered a landslide, since some of the finds also occur below the terraces, on the exceptionally steep slope of the foot of the hill. The pottery finds unambiguously confirm occupation by the Púchov culture, as do the metal finds, which were almost exclusively of iron (apart from two bronze amulets).
The most interesting finds from the fortification include above all a bronze basket-shaped pendant and a figurine of a ram.

The shape of this kind of pendant, as B. M. Pomberger points out, derives from Hallstatt models. This author dates the earliest examples as early as the HB3 phase (the site of Simaság in Hungary), with uninterrupted continuation into the La Tène period. In the area of the Púchov culture this is a very typical kind of openwork pendant of spherical to cylindrical shapes with a hollow interior, which was produced by casting. The shape of this type of amulet recalls rattles, and it is not out of the question that they really were intended to produce sound during the performance of certain rites. Today we can no longer specify the function of these amulets precisely, but they could have served not only at rites but also as personal protective amulets. As the find from the princely grave in the Býčí skála cave suggests, they could also have formed part of funerary rites. The amulet discovered at Gábrišová was precisely such a Hallstatt artefact, known across the Urnfield cultures. Although in shape it derives from these older pendants, its elaboration in the form of arms decorated with pea-like bosses places it, on the basis of other, almost identical pendants from Liptovská Mara I-Havránok and Liptovská Mara III, in the Late La Tène period. Further similar amulets likewise come from the territory of the Púchov culture, from Blatnica and Folkušová.
The bronze figurine of a ram

Zoomorphic figurines depicting miniatures of the attribute animals venerated by the Celts belong, in terms of symbolism, among the readable objects. Figurines of young bulls and of dogs occur most frequently. Since in the area of the Púchov culture we have no record of grave finds, the question of how such amulets were worn remains a matter of speculation. It is, however, very probable that together with other pendants they formed part of necklaces. From the territory of Slovakia some 20 similar amulets have so far been documented, and only a small proportion of them come from stratified finds, in a few cases from hoards – Udiča, Kolačno and Plavecké Podhradie. The hoards from the last two sites named also contained other components of necklaces. For this reason the interpretation of animal figurines as their main components appears very probable. Among the most recent additions to this category must be counted the bronze figurine of a ram with a suspension loop found during the investigation at Gábrišová. Among the Slovak finds, this example is most closely resembled by a figurine from the hillfort of Košeca-Nozdrovice. The figurine of a ram can be dated only broadly to the LTC2–LTD2 phases. The dating rests on the accompanying finds, above all on pottery of the La Tène phase of the Púchov culture.

Other interesting finds from the fortification include iron knives, a ploughshare and structural fittings. Ploughshares, as a rule of iron, formed the extended part of the ard, which broke up the soil at a certain angle. Ploughshares are a fairly common find at La Tène and Early Roman sites in Slovakia. This fact testifies to the circumstance that, unlike some other implements, ploughshares demonstrably underwent changes in form. In principle we distinguish two types of ploughshare: narrow and broad, with a developmental intermediate between them in the form of narrow ploughshares with a leaf-shaped widened tip. Three ploughshares come from the archaeological sites of the Púchov culture included in the assemblage under study. One of them belongs to the narrow single-socketed ploughshares with a regularly tapering tip, above which two indistinct lobes are placed for a better attachment of the wooden structure of the ard. This is the find discovered at Gábrišová and at the same time the only one of its kind in the Žilina Basin. The closest analogies are known from Považská Bystrica-Malý Manín and Liptovská Mara I-Havránok, where thanks to well-recorded stratigraphy we can place these ploughshares chronologically in the LTD1 phase. Their emergence is probably connected with the need to work heavier soils, such as occur abundantly precisely in the north and north-west of Slovakia.

Structural fittings form a separate group of finds. They were connected with the working of wood and with the production of objects from it. Since they are iron objects, difficult to date on their own, it is necessary to take into account their find circumstances and the accompanying finds. They occur at many sites of the Púchov culture and have various dimensions, but in general they are iron objects with two arms bent at right angles, very often tapering to a point, which indicates that they were used as fastening material in buildings, but also for the purpose of strengthening wooden products such as small chests or various boxes. They could have fulfilled a function similar to that of nails and wedges, but perhaps it was precisely their shape that could ensure a better cohesion of the joined materials. They are a fairly common find at sites of the Púchov culture. Structural fittings occurred in large numbers at the site of Gábrišová and are attested at the nearby site of Hradské as well. In the wider area of the Púchov culture they are known from the sites of Prosné-Zlatý kôň (2 items) and Udiča-Klapov (3 items). They also occurred very frequently at the oppidum of Manching, thanks to which G. Jacobi divided them into several variants according to their presumed use. For instance, cramps with a shorter body and long points were in his view used as part of a square door lock. One such cramp, precisely with a flat square mount, was found on one of the terraces at the site of Gábrišová. The other cramps from this site were found on their own, without other fittings; some are small, their body, without the bent arms, measuring about 5–8 cm, others are larger, and the length of the arms is also considerably variable. Some cramps have a longer body and short arms, others, conversely, a shorter body and long arms. Examples were even discovered with exceptionally long arms, which were bent twice over so that they overlapped one another, thus forming a kind of square-shaped collar. This variability in proportions indicates a truly broad-spectrum use. At no site other than Gábrišová is such a high number of this kind of find attested, although, as has already been stated above, they occur at several sites of the Púchov culture.

Pieces of iron slag are a more or less common find in the layers of the Púchov culture in the Žilina Basin as well. They are found at several sites in Malá Čierna, Nezbudská Lúčka and Závodie. In north-western Slovakia, however, only the metallurgical installations at the site of Železná studňa at Varín have so far been archaeologically investigated, and most recently similar installations have been examined at Bánová, Ovčiarne and Bitarová-Rybník. The evidence for the smelting of haematite at Varín consists above all of oval heaps of metallurgical waste, whose dimensions reached about 15 × 23 m, with a maximum height estimated at 1.5 m. Destroyed furnaces were discovered in the form of collapsed domes and fragments of burnt grates. As part of the production process, channels, a high concentration of iron slag and, not least, metallurgical implements were also discovered in the field. On the basis of the find circumstances from the archaeological excavation, these were furnaces with slag tapping, with production dated by C14 to the range from the middle of the 1st century to the beginning of the 2nd century AD. The activity is nevertheless assumed as early as the end of the La Tène period, given the character of the occupation of the region. Above all thick-walled vessels with fused residues. Unfortunately, not one of the furnaces could be investigated in situ, and the excavation likewise did not verify the number of metallurgical installations. The authors of the excavation assume that after the end of each smelting season the furnace, or furnaces, were demolished in order to keep the production secret. Besides the authors of the excavation, the iron-working activity at Železná studňa at Varín was studied by M. Giertlová-Kučerová in her master's thesis. From the point of view of archaeobotanical finds the site was assessed by M. Hajnalová, who drew attention, among other things, to the fact that in the past oak and hornbeam woods grew at the site, or in its immediate vicinity. Today the area is forested rather with coniferous trees, and part of the site consists of grassy pastures. The iron ore processed at Varín came from the haematite source in the Rechtorská dolina valley, at the site of Rudy. Analyses of slag from the find spot confirmed the exceptional technological sophistication and skill of the smelters of the Púchov culture, which agrees with the accounts of classical authors. Similar metallurgical installations are assumed at Nezbudská Lúčka as well (the site of Pri Háji), where numerous finds of slag and pottery of the earlier phase of the Roman period have been appearing for many years now. Further rich finds of iron slag are also known from the site of Baňa at Nezbudská Lúčka and at the mouth of the local stream into the bed of the Váh at the site of Hradská dolina (not far from Starhrad). The accompanying pottery finds are all consistently dated to the 1st century AD. If excavation were in future to succeed in confirming the processing of iron ore at these sites neighbouring Železná studňa, it would without doubt be an exceptionally important and extensive centre of metallurgy of the Púchov culture. In the present state of knowledge, however, there is no sufficient evidence that would unambiguously confirm such a theory. During the excavation at the site of Železná studňa no dwelling features were discovered that would indicate the existence of a contemporary settlement inhabited by the smelters operating the pyrotechnological installations. Nor has any settlement so far been known in the wider surroundings, with the possible exception of a single hamlet at the site of Strečno-Hradný vrch, where the remains of features with pottery dated to the B1 phase were recorded. The question thus arose as to where the craftsmen working in these extensive workshops in the Varín area were settled. Perhaps this riddle has been partly answered by the recent discovery of the terraced settlement at the site of Gábrišová. This could be connected with the iron-working centre at Železná studňa. Extraction took place here as late as the last century. At Gábrišová, however, only an informative metal-detector survey has so far been carried out, from which we know La Tène pottery – graphite situla-shaped vessels and pot-shaped forms. The metal objects from there show a rather Late La Tène origin, or else are not chronologically sensitive. It is not out of the question, however, that more intensive excavation would demonstrate the survival of the settlement even after the turn of the eras. There is convincing evidence of the skill of the people of the Púchov culture in the working of iron, which agrees with the accounts of classical authors. Besides the investigated site at Železná studňa at Varín, indications are also known of further sites in the vicinity of Železná studňa (e.g. Baňa and Lúky pod Jedľovinou), which suggest the existence of a large centre for the processing of iron ore in the Strečno gorge, close to natural sources of iron ore. The fortification with the settlement on the terraces of Gábrišová perhaps complements the settlement structure, and it may be assumed with high probability that it was precisely here that the craftsmen who processed the ore at the nearby Železná studňa lived.
